cues.text: Let's turn now to automation tools and strategy.
Once you understand what testing is and why it matters, the natural next question is: which tools do we use to automate it, and how do we decide what to automate in the first place?
We will begin with the tools, and then move to the strategy.
The source gives us a table with two columns.
The first column is headed Tool, and the second is headed Use.
There are six rows, and I will walk through them in order.
Row one.
The tools are unittest, pytest, JUnit and Jest.
Their use is unit tests and other programmatic tests.
So these are the frameworks you write your tests in, in code.
Unittest and pytest are associated with Python, JUnit with Java, and Jest with JavaScript.
The source lists them together as tools for unit and other programmatic tests.
Row two.
Selenium WebDriver and Selenium Grid.
Their use is web UI automation and cross-browser testing.
WebDriver drives a web user interface automatically, and Grid is listed alongside it for running that kind of testing across different browsers.
Row three.
Appium.
Its use is mobile testing, covering native, hybrid and web applications.
Row four.
JMeter.
Its use is load and performance testing.
That means checking how a system behaves under demand, rather than whether a single function returns the right value.
Row five.
Postman and Newman.
Their use is API test collections.
You group requests to an application programming interface into collections, and those collections can be run as tests.
Row six.
CI pipelines.
CI stands for continuous integration.
Their use is to run checks on changes and report results.
So whenever code changes, the pipeline runs the checks and tells you what happened.
Now, the strategy.
The source begins with a balanced statement: automation improves repeatability, speed and feedback, but it has costs.
Those costs are setup, maintenance, and false positives or flakiness.
A false positive is a test that reports a problem when there is none.
A flaky test is one that gives inconsistent results.
So automation is valuable, but never free.
Next is the test pyramid.
It favours many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and fewer end-to-end UI tests.
Picture a pyramid with a wide base of unit tests, a narrower middle of integration tests, and a small top of end-to-end UI tests.
The source adds an important qualification: adapt this to your architecture.
It is a guide, not a rigid rule.
On what to automate: automate stable, repetitive and risk-critical paths.
But retain exploratory testing and human usability testing.
Some things need a person's judgement and curiosity.
On tool style: low-code tools suit simpler workflows, while scripts offer control for complex integrations, performance and security work.
For good practice, the source lists four points.
Use deterministic test environments, meaning the same setup produces the same results.
Use isolated data, so tests do not interfere with each other.
Use stable selectors, which are the ways a test locates elements on a page.
And use meaningful assertions, meaning checks that actually confirm something important.
Now a subtle warning about self-healing locator tools.
These tools may keep tests running while validating the wrong behaviour.
A test can stay green and still be checking the wrong thing.
So the source requires three safeguards: review of changes, traceability, and business outcome assertions.
Its example is this: check for the correct endpoint and data, not just that a button was clicked.
Clicking a button proves little.
What matters is that the right result happened.
Let us move on to measurement.
The source says to measure meaningful coverage, defects detected and escaped, duration, flake rate and maintenance cost.
Defects detected are those your testing caught.
Escaped defects are those that got past testing.
Flake rate is how often tests give inconsistent results.
Here is the source's example.
If test time drops by 80 percent, but failures occur in untested paths, then you should optimise coverage and risk, not speed alone.
A fast suite that misses the failing paths is not a good suite.
On maintenance: retire redundant and obsolete tests, repair fragile tests, and preserve essential coverage.
Removing tests is fine, but never at the cost of coverage that matters.
Next, AI prioritisation.
When tests are prioritised using historical defects, it can miss new architectural risks, because history cannot show you risks in a design that is new.
So the source says to combine three things: recent change impact, dependency mapping, and expert review.
Finally, machine learning systems.
They need model and data versioning, representative performance and fairness tests, drift monitoring, and reproducibility.
And note this last qualification carefully: changed training data can alter predictions even without code changes or randomness.
So if the data changes, the behaviour can change, even when the code is untouched.
That is why versioning the data matters as much as versioning the code.
